metadata.name: User profiles on MySQL: replica lag and stale reads
metadata.description: A user-profile service. A mobile app (65% of requests, one retry) and a web app (35%) call a Go profile API on four instances behind a load balancer. MySQL 8 runs a primary for writes and three read replicas that serve every read; each replica applies the primary's changes on 4 worker threads (replica_parallel_workers, MySQL 8's default), at about 70% of the original write's time. 1,500 req/s over 200,000 users, 10% of them profile and settings updates. Replication is asynchronous, so the request path says little here: a replica can fall seconds behind while every request succeeds, and a replica read of a profile whose latest change it has not applied yet is stale. All numbers are illustrative assumptions.

edges.label: reads from the replicas, writes to the primary

scenarios.name: Normal day
scenarios.description: The document as drawn: 1,500 req/s, 150 of them updates. Replaying a write takes about 4.5 ms, so each replica's 4 workers could apply about 890 a second: the lag stays under about 15 ms and 13 of about 67,000 replica reads are stale. Every request succeeds; p95 is about 185 ms, most of it the mobile network.

scenarios.name: Settings surge: 1,050 updates a second
scenarios.description: The app asks every user to confirm new notification settings: updates go from 150 to 1,050 a second while reads stay at 1,350. The replicas apply about 890 a second and fall behind from the first second: the lag grows by about 0.15 s every second and reaches about 9 s by the end of the run, and 17% of replica reads (11,670 of 67,406) return a profile without its latest change. Every request succeeds and p95 does not move: nothing on the request path shows it. Only the replication-lag finding does.

scenarios.name: Settings surge, 16 apply workers
scenarios.description: The usual fix: replica_parallel_workers = 16, with writeset dependency tracking so that changes to different users can apply in parallel. The replicas now apply the 1,050 writes a second with room to spare: the lag stays under about 30 ms and 122 replica reads (0.2%) are stale, against 11,670 with 4 workers. Nothing else changes: the request path looked the same before.

scenarios.name: Settings surge, reads from the primary
scenarios.description: The blunt fix for stale reads: send every read to the primary. No read is stale, but the primary now runs 1,350 reads and 1,050 writes a second on its own 4 vCPUs and 16 connections, while the three replicas replay writes nobody reads (they still fall 7 s behind). Its CPU is nearly full and its connection queue overflows: about 3% of requests fail (7.7% of the web app's; the mobile app's retry gets all but 0.7% through) and p95 rises to about 450 ms.

scenarios.name: Storage stall: 5× slower for 20 s (25–45 s)
scenarios.description: Chaos on a normal day: every query, log flush and replay on the database is 5× slower for 20 s, as when an EBS volume runs out of I/O credits. At 150 updates a second, replay now needs about 3.4 of each replica's 4 workers, and the replicas fall up to 1.6 s behind: 388 replica reads are stale instead of 13. Users barely notice: every request succeeds and p95 inside the window rises from 185 to 223 ms. The lag clears about 2 s after the stall ends.

value.label: EBS volume out of I/O credits
